description: Bilim, teknoloji ve uzay araştırmaları odağında yenilikçi çözümler geliştirmek için NASA Space Apps Challenge kapsamında bir araya geldik. Takımımızla birlikte üretmeye, keşfetmeye ve geleceğe yön verecek fikirler geliştirmeye hazırız!
summary:
Abandoned but not Forgotten — NASA Hardware Simulation

Since the 1960s NASA has left hardware across the solar system, but to a school-age audience these objects are either “space junk” or names they have never heard. We turned that hardware into something a K-12 student can handle: a single-file, offline-capable, bilingual (Turkish/English) interactive simulation plus teacher guide.

The package covers 22 hardware records — Apollo descent stages, ALSEP stations, the laser retroreflectors, Surveyor 3, the Ranger impactors, Viking, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity, entry-descent-landing debris, Curiosity, Perseverance, Voyager 1 and 2, Pioneer 10, New Horizons and Cassini/Galileo — each as a card linked to its NASA source. It adds draggable 3D maps of the Moon, Mars and deep space, and seven physics simulations (signal delay, RTG power budget, dust on solar panels, laser ranging, seismograph, rover race, flight on Mars) that let students compute the science the hardware made possible.

Why it matters: a child does not read “why did this robot go quiet?” — they drag the slider and find out. The Story Workshop then tags writing as [FACT] or [FICTION], building scientific honesty into the storytelling itself.
details:
What it does and how it works

The app has nine sections:

  1. Challenge Brief — the official challenge statement (English original plus Turkish translation), what the challenge asks for, a suggested first-hour workflow, and how the package maps onto the Space Apps judging criteria.
  2. 3D Map — the Moon and Mars are rendered as spheres you drag to rotate and scroll to zoom. Markers sit at real coordinates (Tranquility Base 0.674°N / 23.473°E; Jezero 18.44°N / 77.45°E). The deep-space tab uses a logarithmic scale — each division is ten times farther.
  3. Hardware Catalog — 22 cards on one shared template: What it is / The science it made possible / What was left behind and its status today / A surprising fact. Five status classes: still working, passive but still in use, silent and resting in place, deliberately impacted, drifting away.
  4. Seven simulations — each displays its formula openly and ends with an “outcome check” question:
    • Signal Delay: t = d/c, c = 299,792.458 km/s. Includes Voyager 1 reaching exactly one light-day (25.902 billion km) on 18 November 2026; the animation runs in real time or sped up.
    • Power Budget (RTG): P(y) ≈ 470 W · 0.5^((y−1977)/87.7) · (1 − 0.006·(y−1977)) — drag the year slider and Voyager’s instruments switch off one by one.
    • Dust and solar panels: E ≈ 900 Wh · (1 − dust) · e^(−0.33·(τ − 0.5)). The “2018 storm” preset drives τ to ≈10.8 and energy down to 22 Wh/sol, Opportunity’s final value.
    • Laser Ranging: the Apollo retroreflectors; distance computed from round-trip time, plus the Moon’s ~3.8 cm/year recession.
    • Seismograph: P and S waves drawn on canvas; d ≈ Δt · 8.4 km/s. Compares the Moon (ALSEP, ~12,000 events) with Mars (InSight, 1,300+ marsquakes).
    • Rover Race: a 1969→2026 year slider, including Perseverance passing Opportunity’s 45.16 km record with 45.22 km on 11 October 2026.
    • Flight on Mars: T ∝ ρ·(rpm)², W = m·g; a Mars/Earth toggle shows why Ingenuity needed ~2,500 rpm.
  5. Status Sorting — a click-to-classify game.
  6. Timeline 1964 → 2026.
  7. Story Workshop — the student picks a machine, ticks the verified facts they want to use, then writes in first or third person against five prompts (Who am I? What was my mission? My greatest discovery? My end? Why do I matter today?). In the preview, facts are tagged [FACT] and imagination [FICTION]; the text can be copied or downloaded as .txt. A five-item self-assessment checklist accompanies it.
  8. Ten-question quiz — each answer reveals its explanation.
  9. K-12 Outcomes — four grade bands (K-2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-12) with tables mapping NGSS, CCSS, ISTE and Turkish MEB codes, plus a module-to-outcome matrix.

A ten-module progress bar sits in the header and persists through localStorage, so a student can close the page and come back.

Benefits and intended impact

A teacher can walk into class with no preparation: open the file, pick the grade band, read the outcome codes, run one simulation and one writing activity. The student is not a passive reader — they drag a slider, kill Opportunity with their own hands, then write about why it died. The intended impact has three layers: (a) knowing the hardware’s name and story, (b) grasping the underlying physics numerically, and (c) being able to argue the question “is abandoned hardware litter or heritage?” — which maps directly onto MEB F.7.1.1.2 (space pollution) and NGSS HS-ETS1-3 (ethical trade-offs).

The single-file, offline decision is an access decision: in low-bandwidth schools it opens from a tablet or a USB stick, with no install, no account and no internet.

Tools used

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3 (custom properties for theming), vanilla JavaScript (ES6+). No external libraries, CDNs or build step — one .html file, ~206 KB.
  • Graphics: hand-written SVG; <canvas> with requestAnimationFrame for the seismogram and the 3D bodies (our own small rotation/projection routine and procedural surface-texture generator).
  • Data: all hardware records, outcomes, quiz items and sources are embedded as JSON structures inside the file, with an i18n dictionary for instant TR/EN switching.
  • Persistence: localStorage.
  • Verification: NSSDCA Master Catalog, NASA Science mission pages, JPL news releases, the LROC and HiRISE archives, PDS Geosciences.

Creativity and what the team considered

  • Physics as mechanics, not decoration: every simulation shows its formula on screen, and the numbers are anchored to real NASA values (τ = 10.8; 22 Wh/sol; 87.7-year half-life; 45.22 km; 2,400–2,900 rpm; 128.8 minutes aloft).
  • Fact/fiction separation is built into the design: writing is free, but the output is automatically tagged [FACT] / [FICTION]. The challenge asks us to introduce the science; we placed narrative beside it rather than in its place.
  • Copyright hygiene: we embedded no NASA photographs. Every visual is an original SVG or canvas drawing we made ourselves; NASA’s image archives are credited by link. The footer states plainly that the package was produced independently and is neither created nor endorsed by NASA.
  • We did not hide uncertainty: deep-space distances are marked approximate (≈); the 3D surface textures are noted as procedurally generated, not NASA imagery; the RTG and thrust models are labelled as simplified.
  • Accessibility: visible keyboard focus, two languages, a high-contrast dark theme, responsive layout, offline operation.
  • Localization: alongside the US standards (NGSS/CCSS/ISTE) we mapped Turkish MEB codes and added a transition note for the 2024 “Türkiye Yüzyılı Maarif Modeli” — so the package is genuinely usable in our own classroom.
